subject: 29,000 jobs, and the Fed still might hike again
bodyMarkdown:
The US added 29,000 jobs in September, and the strange part is that the Federal Reserve might still raise rates on October 28. If you have a mortgage renewal coming or any money in a bond fund, that combination is worth three minutes this morning.

## The revisions were worse than the headline

Bloomberg reported on Friday that US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, against forecasts closer to 84,000, and that the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2 per cent from 4.1. The back months are where it gets ugly. Forbes reported on Friday that July's original gain of 21,000 was rewritten into a loss of 10,000, and that July and August together were cut by 60,000 jobs. That drops the recent average to roughly 45,000 a month, which is closer to treading water than to hiring. Pay is going backwards too. Average hourly earnings reached 37.81 US dollars, up 3.0 per cent over the year, while US consumer prices rose 3.4 per cent in the twelve months to August.

## Why a hike is still on the table

Here is the part people forget. CNBC reported that the Fed raised its target range to 3.75 to 4 per cent on September 16, its first increase since 2023, ending a five-meeting pause. Chase's summary of that meeting said officials signalled one more increase before the end of the year. Then Friday arrived and the betting moved fast. Kalshi and Polymarket put a hold on October 28 at roughly 84 per cent and a quarter-point hike near 17. I think one soft month settles less than the market assumes. **Core inflation**, which strips out food and fuel to show the underlying trend, has run above 3 per cent on the Fed's preferred PCE measure every month of 2026, even though core CPI was a milder 2.4 per cent in August. The two disagree, and the Fed is leaning on the hotter one. September CPI lands October 14, and I would watch that harder than Friday's jobs print.

## Ottawa decides the same day

The Bank of Canada announces at 9:45 am Eastern on October 28, the same day the Fed finishes, with a Monetary Policy Report attached. Our rate has sat at 2.25 per cent since October 2025. Canada's case for a hike looks weaker than America's to me. Statistics Canada reported on September 14 that inflation held at 3.0 per cent in August, but the Bank's own core measures came in at 1.9 per cent for CPI-trim and 2.0 per cent for CPI-median, and gasoline at 22.8 per cent year over year did much of the lifting in that headline number. Our labour market is moving the other way. BNN Bloomberg reported on September 4 that the economy shed 42,000 jobs in August and the employment rate slipped to 60.8 per cent, with unemployment at 6.4. Polymarket still had about 61 cents on a hold against 39 on a hike to 2.50 per cent.

## The takeaway

Watch October 9, when Statistics Canada publishes the September jobs numbers, because two weak months in a row would make a Canadian hike very hard to argue for. Then watch US CPI on October 14, which arrives two weeks before both decisions. If you are renewing a mortgage before spring, do not assume the hold survives the winter, since the Bank has said households rolling off five-year fixed terms face payments close to 20 per cent higher. And retire the old reflex that a bad jobs report means cheaper money, because in 2026 it mostly means a slower economy carrying the same inflation.
